To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the immune response elicited and the protection provided by a live vaccine can depend on the route of administration and that the immune response and protection can be different even when the same vaccine strain is used.

(i) oral administration of a live vaccine elicits a secretory Ig response that is not seen in intravenous vaccination; (ii) oral and intravenous vaccination with a live vaccine confer similar levels of protection in terms of suppression of challenge in systemic organs and animal survival; (iii) oral and intravenously-vaccinated mice show differences in suppression of challenge in the gut-associated lymphoid tissues, which may be important in the context of transmission.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the interactions between vaccines and their hosts, and the implications for vaccine effectiveness.
understanding the immune responses elicited in animals by vaccines, and the effect these have on the growth of the vaccine strain.
how vaccination affects the immune system, how this affects bacterial growth and shedding, and how this ultimately influences the ability of the vaccine to protect the host against infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
vaccination method does affect the immune response and bacterial growth in the Salmonella typhimurium animal model of typhoid.
the route of administration can influence the immune response and the growth of a live attenuating vaccine strain, but not the protection it confers.
the route of administration has significant effects on immune responses and bacterial growth, but not protection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the immune responses elicited and the ability to suppress challenge are not the same following different vaccination routes and that these differences are important to consider when assessing vaccine efficacy.
the method of vaccine administration affects both immune stimulation and bacterial growth but not protection in the murine typhoid animal model.
while both vaccination methods are effective at stimulating the immune response and providing protection against systemic infection, they differ in their ability to suppress colonisation of the gut.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the route of vaccine administration can have a significant impact on the immune response and the protection conferred, even when the same vaccine strain is used, and this should be considered in future vaccine design.
while both vaccination methods were equally protective, the oral route was more effective at reducing shedding and transmission.
while vaccines can appear to confer the same level of protection in a challenge model, this may mask differences in their effects on immune responses and pathogen shedding.
